source_key_points: 6 PERIMETER AND AREA 6.1 Perimeter Do you remember what the perimeter of a closed plane figure is?
The perimeter of any closed plane figure is the distance covered along its boundary when you go around it once.
For a polygon, i.e., a closed plane figure made up of line segments, the perimeter is simply the sum of the lengths of its all sides, i.e., the total distance along its outer boundary.
The perimeter of a polygon = the sum of the lengths of its all sides.
Let us revise the formulas for the perimeter of rectangles, squares, and triangles.
Perimeter of a rectangle Consider a rectangle ABCD whose length and breadth are 12 cm and 8 cm, respectively.

Perimeter of the rectangle = Sum of the lengths of its four sides = AB + BC + CD + DA A 12 cm B 8 cm D C Reprint 2026-27 Chapter 6_Perimeter and Area.indd 129 13-08-2024 16:16:29 Ganita Prakash | Grade 6 = AB + BC + AB + BC Opposite sides of a = 2 × AB + 2 × BC rectangle are always = 2 × (AB + BC) equal.
So, AB = CD and = 2 × (12 cm + 8 cm) AD = BC = 2 × (20 cm) = 40 cm.

teacher_explanation.subject: Mathematics
teacher_explanation.content: Class 06 Mathematics Chapter 106: Perimeter and Area focuses on the fundamental concepts of measuring two-dimensional shapes. Perimeter is the total distance around the outside of a shape, calculated by adding the lengths of all its sides. For simple shapes like rectangles, it's P = 2(length + width). Area, on the other hand, is the amount of surface inside a shape, measured in square units. For a rectangle, the formula for area is A = length × width. This chapter introduces various shapes (triangles, squares, parallelograms, etc.) and their corresponding formulas for perimeter and area. It emphasizes the difference between the two concepts and provides step-by-step examples on how to calculate them for real-world scenarios.

concepts.name: Understanding Perimeter
concepts.description: Definition of perimeter as the total length of the boundary of a closed shape. Calculating perimeter of triangles, quadrilaterals, and irregular polygons.

concepts.name: Understanding Area
concepts.description: Definition of area as the amount of two-dimensional surface enclosed by a boundary. Calculating area of triangles, rectangles, squares, and composite shapes.

concepts.name: Perimeter Formulas
concepts.description: Memorizing formulas for common shapes: perimeter of a rectangle (2(l+w)), perimeter of a triangle (a+b+c), perimeter of a parallelogram, and perimeter of irregular polygons.

concepts.name: Area Formulas
concepts.description: Memorizing formulas for common shapes: area of a rectangle (l x w), area of a square (side^2), area of a triangle (0.5 * base * height), area of a parallelogram, and area of composite figures.

concepts.name: Unit Conversion
concepts.description: Converting different units of length and area (e.g., cm to m, sq cm to m²) and understanding that area units are always square units.

concepts.name: Application and Word Problems
concepts.description: Solving real-world problems involving finding missing sides, calculating the cost of fencing (perimeter), and calculating the space needed for materials (area).

story_mode.subject: Mathematics
story_mode.content: Imagine you are a master builder designing a new garden. Your first task is to calculate the perimeter of the garden to determine how much fencing you need to enclose it. The second task is to calculate the area to determine how much soil or grass is required to cover the garden. If the garden is rectangular, you would measure the length and width to find the perimeter (sum of all sides) and the area (length × width). You might encounter a circular flower bed, where you would need to use formulas involving $\pi$ to estimate the circumference (perimeter) and the space covered (area). This story illustrates how perimeter and area are essential tools for planning and construction projects, from fencing boundaries to laying carpets or painting walls.

chapter_summary.subject: Mathematics
chapter_summary.content: Chapter 106, 'Perimeter and Area', provides a comprehensive guide to the mathematical concepts of perimeter and area. It establishes that perimeter is the linear measurement of the boundary of a two-dimensional figure, while area is the two-dimensional measurement of the surface enclosed by that boundary. The chapter covers formulas for polygons (square, rectangle, triangle) and introduces area calculations for circles. Mastery of these concepts is fundamental for solving practical problems in geometry and various real-world applications involving measuring boundaries and surface coverage.
